newsitem.title: USA: AT&T subscribers can whine their way to dime a minute.
newsitem.headline: AT&T subscribers can whine their way to dime a minute.

text.p: AT&T Corp. customers who make more than 100 minutes a month in long-distance calls would do well to insist on being transferred to a new and unpublicised calling plan called One Rate Plus.
One Rate Plus costs $4.95 per month but charges only a flat 10 cents per minute day or night, seven days a week.
AT&T confirmed the existence of the calling plan following an article in the Wall Street Journal on Thursday.
"It is just one promotion that seems to have hit the spotlight at the moment," said Karyn Vaughn-Fritz, an AT&T spokeswoman.
A call to AT&T's customer service representatives proved that subscribers who ask for the new plan have to complain and insist just to get them to acknowledge existence of the new plan.

AT&T's heavily advertised 15 cent per minute One Rate plan, introduced last last year, has no monthly charge. To cover the monthly fee, subcribers need to make 100 minutes a month in long distance calls before they start to save money.
Vaughn-Fritz said AT&T had received a steady stream of new callers since the Wall Street Journal story appeared, but said the company was sticking to its criteria for switching users.
"We are only doing this on a case-by-case basis, for our most-valued customers," she said.
Vaughn-Fritz confirmed that old bills are the yardstick, but would not say how big the bills had to be to qualify.
However, AT&T did confirm that for "particularly valued" customers, the $4.95 per month fee would be waived for the first couple of months.
For big spenders on international and long distance calling, there are more and more good deals around.
Sprint Corp. was the first with dime-a-minute calling, but that was only for off-peak calls.
MCI Communications Corp. now offers 12 cents a minute for those subscribers who spend at least $25 per month with MCI.
However, those who don't bargain get left behind.
Old calling plans, many of which still have millions of subscribers, tend to get pricier when overtaken by a new plan.
Industry analysts say all the long distance companies, struggling to survive in a cutthroat market, are taking the classic approach of segmenting the marketplace.
This means getting those who are insensitive to price to pay the high rates, but offer low rates to hard bargainers who threaten to go to a rival.
